title: Management Accounting

pattern.summary: Section A: answer 2 of 3 (theory; Q3 is short notes, any 4 of 6). Section B: answer 3 of 5 or 6 — mostly sums on ratios, budgets, variances, CVP and marginal costing. Each question 20 marks.

choosing: Section A: Q3 short notes is usually the easiest 20 marks — you choose 4 of 6.
Section B: budgets, variances and CVP sums appear in almost every paper; marginal-costing decisions (make or buy, sales mix) are frequent.
Many Section B questions are half theory, half sum — pick those if your numericals are weaker.
numerical: Mark every variance F or A and check that the parts add up to the total.
Show fixed and variable costs separately in budgets and marginal cost statements.

blocks.title: Management Accounting: Introduction and Basic Techniques
Marginal Costing and Cost Volume Profit Analysis

topics.name: Standard Costing & Variance Analysis
topics.summary: Meaning, objectives, advantages and limitations of standard costing; standard costing vs budgeting and estimate costing; material and labour variances.
points: Standard costing: setting predetermined costs for each element, comparing actual costs with them and analysing the differences (variances) for control.
Objectives and advantages: cost control, measuring efficiency, fixing responsibility, management by exception, pricing and budgeting help, cost consciousness, simpler stock valuation.
Limitations: setting accurate standards is hard, standards date quickly, costly for small firms, may demotivate if too tight, not suited to job work.
Standard costing vs budgeting: unit-level vs total; mainly production costs vs all functions; a technique of cost control vs a planning tool; variances analysed by cause vs totals compared.
Estimate costing vs standard costing: estimates are guesses of what costs will be (for quotations), standards are what costs should be (for control), set scientifically.
Material variances: cost = price + usage; usage = mix + yield (or sub-usage). Labour variances: cost = rate + efficiency (+ idle time); efficiency = mix + sub-efficiency.

Overhead variances (Unit 12): variable overhead — expenditure and efficiency; fixed overhead — expenditure and volume (volume = capacity + efficiency, plus calendar). Sales variances: price and volume (volume = mix + quantity).
mistakes: Forgetting to mark each variance favourable (F) or adverse (A).
Using standard quantity for total input instead of standard quantity for actual output.
method: Find standard quantity (or hours) for actual output: scale the standard to the actual output or yield.
Material cost variance = standard cost of actual output − actual cost.
Price variance = AQ × (SP − AP); usage variance = SP × (SQ − AQ).
Mix variance = SP × (revised standard quantity − AQ), where RSQ = actual total input in the standard ratio.
Yield variance = standard cost per unit of output × (actual yield − standard yield from actual input).
For labour, repeat with hours and rates; check rate + efficiency = cost variance.
formula: MCV = (SQ × SP) − (AQ × AP)
MPV = AQ × (SP − AP)
MUV = SP × (SQ − AQ)
MMV = SP × (RSQ − AQ)
LCV = (SH × SR) − (AH × AR)
LRV = AH × (SR − AR)
LEV = SR × (SH − AH)
topics.frame: Working table (SQ, SP, AQ, AP) → each variance with formula and F/A → check that parts add up to the total.
examples:
Example: material variances
Standard: 2 kg per unit at ₹10 a kg. Actual output 1,000 units, using 2,100 kg bought at ₹9.50.
Standard quantity for actual output = 2,000 kg; standard cost ₹20,000; actual cost ₹19,950.
MCV = 20,000 − 19,950 = ₹50 (F).
MPV = 2,100 × (10 − 9.50) = ₹1,050 (F).
MUV = 10 × (2,000 − 2,100) = ₹1,000 (A).
Check: 1,050 F − 1,000 A = 50 F ✓. Buying cheaper saved money, but more material was wasted.

Example: labour variances
Standard: 3 hours per unit at ₹20 an hour. For 1,000 units, 2,900 hours are worked at ₹21.
Standard hours = 3,000; standard cost ₹60,000; actual cost ₹60,900 → LCV ₹900 (A).
LRV = 2,900 × (20 − 21) = ₹2,900 (A). LEV = 20 × (3,000 − 2,900) = ₹2,000 (F).
Check: 2,900 A − 2,000 F = 900 A ✓. Workers were paid more but worked faster.

Example: material mix variance
Standard mix: A 60% at ₹10, B 40% at ₹15. Actual input 200 kg: A 110 kg, B 90 kg.
Revised standard quantity (200 kg in the standard ratio): A 120, B 80.
MMV = 10 × (120 − 110) + 15 × (80 − 90) = 100 − 150 = ₹50 (A) — more of the costlier material B was used.

topics.name: Cost–Volume–Profit & Break-Even Analysis
topics.summary: Contribution, P/V ratio, break-even point, margin of safety, angle of incidence, sales for a target profit and the effect of changes in price and costs.
points: CVP analysis studies how costs, volume and profit are related — it answers questions like 'what sales are needed to break even or to earn ₹X profit?'.
Contribution = sales − variable cost; it covers fixed cost first, then gives profit.
P/V ratio = contribution ÷ sales; a higher ratio means profit grows faster with sales.
Break-even point: sales at which there is no profit or loss. Margin of safety: sales above break-even — a measure of safety.
Angle of incidence: the angle at which the sales line cuts the total cost line on a break-even chart; a large angle shows high profit potential.
Uses: pricing, planning profit, choosing products, make or buy, effect of cost changes. Assumptions: costs split into fixed and variable, constant price and efficiency, one product or constant mix.
mistakes: Mixing P/V ratio as a percentage and as a decimal in the same calculation.
method: Find contribution per unit (or total) and the P/V ratio.
If two years' figures are given: P/V ratio = change in profit ÷ change in sales; then fixed cost = contribution − profit.
BEP = fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio (₹) or ÷ contribution per unit (units).
Sales for target profit = (fixed cost + profit) ÷ P/V ratio.
For a change in price or cost, recompute contribution and P/V ratio, then the new BEP.
formula: P/V ratio = Contribution ÷ Sales × 100 = Change in profit ÷ Change in sales × 100
BEP (₹) = Fixed cost ÷ P/V ratio
BEP (units) = Fixed cost ÷ Contribution per unit
Margin of safety = Actual sales − BEP sales = Profit ÷ P/V ratio
Required sales = (Fixed cost + Desired profit) ÷ P/V ratio
topics.frame: Write the formula, substitute, answer with units (₹ or units) — one line per part.
examples:
Example: P/V ratio, break-even and margin of safety
Sales ₹10,00,000; variable cost ₹6,00,000; fixed cost ₹3,00,000.
Contribution ₹4,00,000; P/V ratio 40%; profit ₹1,00,000.
BEP = 3,00,000 ÷ 40% = ₹7,50,000. Margin of safety = 10,00,000 − 7,50,000 = ₹2,50,000 (check: profit ÷ P/V = 1,00,000 ÷ 40%).
Sales needed for a profit of ₹2,00,000 = (3,00,000 + 2,00,000) ÷ 40% = ₹12,50,000.

Example: two years' figures given
Year 1: sales ₹8,00,000, profit ₹50,000. Year 2: sales ₹10,00,000, profit ₹1,00,000.
P/V ratio = change in profit ÷ change in sales = 50,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 25%.
Fixed cost = contribution − profit = 25% × 8,00,000 − 50,000 = ₹1,50,000. BEP = 1,50,000 ÷ 25% = ₹6,00,000.

topics.name: Budgets & Budgetary Control
topics.summary: Budgeting and budgetary control, objectives, advantages and limitations, types of budgets, flexible budget, cash budget, master and sales budgets, zero-based and performance budgeting, control ratios.
points: Budget: a quantitative plan for a future period. Budgetary control: setting budgets, comparing actuals with them and acting on differences.
Objectives and advantages: planning, coordination, control, fixing responsibility, efficient use of resources, motivation. Limitations: based on estimates, rigid, costly, needs support of staff.

Types: by time (long-term, short-term), by function (sales, production, materials, labour, overhead, cash, capital expenditure), by flexibility (fixed, flexible); master budget combines all functional budgets.

Flexible budget: shows costs at different levels of activity by separating fixed, variable and semi-variable costs. Steps: decide activity levels, classify costs, compute each at every level, find the overhead rate.

Cash budget: estimates cash receipts and payments to find surpluses or shortages. Methods: receipts and payments (short term), adjusted profit and loss (start from profit, add non-cash items, adjust working capital and capital items — long term), balance sheet method.
Zero-based budgeting: every activity is justified from zero each year rather than adding to last year's budget — cuts waste, links spending to priorities.
Performance budgeting: budgets linked to programmes, activities and measurable outputs; process — define programmes, set targets and performance measures, allocate funds, review results.
Control ratios: capacity ratio = actual hours ÷ budgeted hours; activity ratio = standard hours for actual output ÷ budgeted hours; efficiency ratio = standard hours ÷ actual hours.
mistakes: Keeping fixed costs per unit constant across levels — fixed cost in total is constant.
method: Classify each cost as fixed, variable or semi-variable (split semi-variable into fixed and variable).
Variable cost at each level = rate per unit × units; fixed stays the same.
Total the costs at each level; divide by units or hours for the rate.
Cash budget: opening balance + receipts − payments = closing balance, month by month (with time lags for debtors and creditors).
formula: Capacity ratio = Actual hours ÷ Budgeted hours × 100
Activity ratio = Standard hours for actual output ÷ Budgeted hours × 100
Efficiency ratio = Standard hours ÷ Actual hours × 100
topics.frame: Budget in columns for each activity level; state fixed, variable and semi-variable items separately.
examples:
Example: flexible budget
Capacity 10,000 units. Variable cost ₹20 a unit; semi-variable ₹20,000 fixed + ₹3 a unit; fixed ₹1,00,000.
At 60% (6,000 units): 1,20,000 + 38,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹2,58,000 → ₹43 a unit.
At 80% (8,000 units): 1,60,000 + 44,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹3,04,000 → ₹38 a unit.
At 100% (10,000 units): 2,00,000 + 50,000 + 1,00,000 = ₹3,50,000 → ₹35 a unit — unit cost falls as fixed costs are spread.

Example: a month of a cash budget, and control ratios
Opening cash ₹20,000 + cash sales 30,000 + collection of last month's credit sales 50,000 − paid to creditors 40,000 − wages 15,000 − rent 5,000 − machine 30,000 = closing ₹10,000.
Control ratios: budgeted hours 10,000; actual hours 9,000; standard hours for actual output 9,900.
Capacity = 9,000/10,000 = 90%; activity = 9,900/10,000 = 99%; efficiency = 9,900/9,000 = 110%. (Activity = capacity × efficiency: 0.9 × 1.1 = 0.99.)

topics.name: Marginal Costing & Decision Making
topics.summary: Marginal costing and its characteristics, absorption vs marginal income statements, and decisions — make or buy, sales mix, price cuts, special or export orders, differential costing.
points: Marginal costing: only variable costs are charged to products; fixed costs are treated as period costs and written off against contribution.
Characteristics: costs split into fixed and variable; stocks valued at variable cost; contribution used to judge products; profit = contribution − fixed cost.

Absorption vs marginal profits: the same when production equals sales (no change in stock); different when stock changes — absorption profit is higher when production exceeds sales, because some fixed overhead is carried forward in closing stock.
Make or buy: buy if the purchase price is below the variable (marginal) cost of making, considering spare capacity, quality and supply.
Sales mix: choose the mix that gives the highest total contribution (or contribution per unit of the limiting factor).
Price reduction or special/export order: accept if the price covers marginal cost and adds contribution, if capacity is spare and the home market is not harmed.
Differential costing: comparing the change in costs and revenues between alternatives — used for choosing between options.
mistakes: Including fixed costs that do not change in make-or-buy comparisons.
method: Separate variable and fixed costs.
For each option, compute contribution (or total cost of making vs buying).
Compare contributions (or the limiting factor contribution) and choose the higher one.
Absorption statement: include fixed overhead in product cost and value stock at full cost; marginal: stock at variable cost, fixed cost in full.
formula: Contribution = Sales − Variable cost
Profit = Contribution − Fixed cost
topics.frame: Marginal cost statement: Sales − Variable cost = Contribution − Fixed cost = Profit, for each option compared.
examples:
Example: make or buy
Making a component costs: materials ₹20, labour ₹15, variable overhead ₹5, share of fixed overhead ₹10 = ₹50. A supplier offers it at ₹45.
The fixed overhead continues either way, so compare the variable cost ₹40 with ₹45 → make it; buying would lose ₹5 a unit. (If the spare capacity could earn more elsewhere, that must also be counted.)

Example: limiting factor, and absorption vs marginal profit
Machine hours are scarce. Product A: contribution ₹60, 3 hours → ₹20 an hour. Product B: contribution ₹40, 1 hour → ₹40 an hour. Make B first.
Production 10,000 units, sales 8,000; fixed overhead ₹1,00,000 (₹10 a unit). Under absorption costing, closing stock of 2,000 units carries ₹20,000 of fixed overhead forward, so absorption profit is ₹20,000 higher than marginal-costing profit this year.

topics.name: Financial Statements & Their Analysis
topics.summary: Nature, usefulness and limitations of financial statements, tools of analysis, horizontal and vertical balance sheets, profit levels (GP to PAT, profit for equity), reserves and provisions, fund flow statement.
points: Financial statements: balance sheet, statement of profit and loss, cash flow statement and notes. Nature: recorded facts, accounting conventions and personal judgement.
Limitations: historical costs, ignore qualitative factors and inflation, interim not final, window dressing possible, one-year view.
Usefulness for decisions: judge profitability, liquidity and solvency; compare with past and with others; plan and control.
Tools of analysis: comparative statements, common-size statements, trend analysis (index numbers from a base year), ratio analysis, fund flow and cash flow statements.
Horizontal balance sheet: liabilities and assets side by side (T-form). Vertical: one below the other, as in Schedule III.

Profit levels: gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold; operating profit = gross profit − operating expenses; PBIT = operating profit + non-operating income − non-operating expenses; PBT = PBIT − interest; PAT = PBT − tax; profit for equity = PAT − preference dividend.

Reserves are appropriations of profit (revenue, capital, general); provisions are charges against profit for known liabilities or losses. A secret reserve is hidden by undervaluing assets or overvaluing liabilities. Capital reserve comes from capital profits (e.g. premium, profit on reissue of forfeited shares).
Fund flow statement: shows sources and uses of working capital — useful for planning finance; limited because it ignores cash and is historical.
method: Net sales = gross sales − returns inwards.
Gross profit = net sales − cost of goods sold (direct costs).
Operating profit = GP − administrative, selling and distribution expenses.
PBIT = operating profit + non-operating income − non-operating expenses (excluding interest).
PBT = PBIT − interest; PAT = PBT − tax; profit for equity = PAT − preference dividend.
topics.frame: Meaning → headed points → conclusion; for profit levels, show a vertical statement.
examples:
Example: levels of profit
Sales 12,00,000 − returns 20,000 = net sales ₹11,80,000. Cost of goods sold 7,00,000 → gross profit ₹4,80,000 (40.7% of net sales).
Less administration 1,00,000 and selling 80,000 → operating profit ₹3,00,000.
Add dividend received 20,000, less loss on sale of an asset 10,000 → PBIT ₹3,10,000.
Less interest 60,000 → PBT ₹2,50,000; tax at 25% → PAT ₹1,87,500; less preference dividend 20,000 → profit for equity shareholders ₹1,67,500.

Example: trend analysis
Sales: 2022 ₹10 lakh, 2023 ₹12 lakh, 2024 ₹15 lakh. With 2022 as base (100), the trend percentages are 100, 120 and 150 — sales grew 50% in two years.

topics.name: Management Accounting: Meaning, Scope & Functions
topics.summary: Meaning, nature, scope, objectives, functions, techniques and role of management accounting, and how it differs from cost and financial accounting.
points: Management accounting: presenting accounting information to help management plan, control and make decisions.
Nature: forward-looking, decision-oriented, selective, no fixed formats, uses cost and financial data and statistical tools.
Scope: financial accounting, cost accounting, budgeting and forecasting, cost control, reporting to management, tax planning, internal audit, statistical analysis.
Objectives and functions: planning, controlling, organising, coordinating, motivating, communicating, interpreting data, helping decisions.
Techniques: financial planning, analysis of financial statements, standard costing, marginal costing, budgetary control, decision accounting, responsibility accounting, MIS.
Role: supplies information, evaluates alternatives, helps fix prices and policies, measures performance.

Vs cost accounting: wider scope (all information) vs costs only; forward-looking vs mainly historical and current. Vs financial accounting: internal vs external users, no statutory format vs prescribed format, parts of the business vs whole.
topics.frame: Definition → headed points → comparison table where asked → conclusion.
examples:
Example: management accounting at work
A factory manager asks whether to run a second shift. The management accountant estimates the extra wages, power and supervision (differential costs), the contribution from extra sales, the cash needed each month (cash budget), and the break-even volume for the shift, then recommends starting it for the peak season only.
None of this appears in the published financial statements — it is forward-looking information prepared for one decision.

topics.name: Cost Control, Cost Reduction & Cost Management
topics.summary: Cost control and its techniques and advantages, cost reduction and its advantages and limitations, their differences, and techniques of cost management.
points: Cost control: keeping costs within set targets or standards — through budgetary control, standard costing, variance analysis, inventory control, quality control.
Advantages of cost control: higher profit, efficient use of resources, cost consciousness, better pricing, competitiveness.
Cost reduction: a real and permanent fall in unit cost without lowering quality — through value analysis, work study, standardisation and simplification, better design, automation, TQM.

Differences: cost control keeps to targets, cost reduction lowers the targets themselves; control is preventive and short-term, reduction is corrective and continuous; control accepts standards, reduction challenges them.
Limitations of cost reduction: can cut quality if careless, needs investment and staff cooperation, gains may be hard to measure.
Cost management: using techniques across the business to manage costs — activity-based costing, target costing, kaizen, life-cycle costing, value-chain analysis, JIT, benchmarking.
topics.frame: Definition → techniques as headings → comparison table → conclusion.

units.title: Cost Control, Cost Reduction and Cost Management

examples:
Example: cost control vs cost reduction
Cost control: the canteen's budget is ₹50,000 a month; the manager checks each month's spending against it and acts on overspending.
Cost reduction: value analysis shows that a metal bracket can be replaced by a plastic one doing the same job ₹5 cheaper. At 1,00,000 units a year this cuts cost by ₹5,00,000 permanently, and the standard itself is lowered.

topics.name: Ratio Analysis
topics.summary: Liquidity, activity, solvency and profitability ratios, the DuPont model, working back figures from given ratios, and limitations of ratio analysis.
points: Liquidity ratios: current ratio (ideal about 2:1), quick or acid-test ratio (ideal about 1:1).
Activity (turnover) ratios: inventory turnover, debtors turnover and average collection period, creditors turnover and average payment period, working capital turnover.
Solvency ratios: debt–equity, capital gearing, interest coverage.
Profitability ratios: gross and net profit ratios, operating ratio, return on capital employed.
DuPont model: return on equity = net profit margin × asset turnover × equity multiplier — shows what drives returns.
Limitations: based on historical and accounting figures, affected by window dressing and inflation, no standard ratio for all firms, ignores qualitative factors.
method: Write down all given ratios and figures.
Work back step by step (e.g. sales → gross profit → cost of goods sold → average stock from the stock turnover ratio).
Use opening/closing relations (closing stock = opening + ₹X) to split average stock.
Compute each asked ratio and comment.
formula: Current ratio = Current assets ÷ Current liabilities
Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory − Prepaid expenses) ÷ Current liabilities
Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold ÷ Average inventory
Average collection period = 365 ÷ Debtors turnover
Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest
Debt–equity = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds
Capital gearing = (Preference capital + Long-term loans) ÷ Equity shareholders' funds
Operating ratio = (Cost of goods sold + Operating expenses) ÷ Net sales × 100
ROE (DuPont) = Net profit margin × Asset turnover × Equity multiplier
topics.frame: Formula → substitution → answer → one-line comment on what the ratio means.
examples:
Example: liquidity ratios
Current assets ₹4,00,000 (including stock ₹1,50,000 and prepaid expenses ₹10,000); current liabilities ₹2,00,000.
Current ratio = 4,00,000 ÷ 2,00,000 = 2 : 1. Quick ratio = (4,00,000 − 1,60,000) ÷ 2,00,000 = 1.2 : 1 — both are comfortable.

Example: working backwards from ratios
Sales ₹12,00,000; gross profit 25% → cost of goods sold ₹9,00,000. Stock turnover 6 times → average stock = 9,00,000 ÷ 6 = ₹1,50,000. If closing stock is ₹20,000 more than opening: opening ₹1,40,000, closing ₹1,60,000.
Debtors turnover 6 times → average collection period = 365 ÷ 6 ≈ 61 days.
DuPont: net profit margin 10% × asset turnover 2 × equity multiplier 1.5 → ROE = 30%.

topics.name: Responsibility Accounting & Performance
topics.summary: Responsibility accounting, cost, revenue, profit and investment centres, how the centre type affects budgeting and reporting, performance measurement, ROI and residual income.
points: Responsibility accounting: organising accounting around managers' responsibilities — each manager is judged on costs and revenues they control.
Centres: cost centre (responsible for costs), revenue centre (revenues), profit centre (both), investment centre (profit and capital invested).
Differs from conventional cost accounting: organised by people and responsibility, not products; only controllable items; used for performance evaluation rather than just product costing.

Choice of centre: decides what is budgeted and reported — cost budgets and variances for cost centres; sales targets for revenue centres; profit statements for profit centres; ROI and residual income for investment centres.
Performance measurement: budget vs actual, variances, ROI, residual income, EVA; it motivates managers and fixes accountability.
Residual income (RI) = profit − (investment × cost of capital). Unlike ROI, it encourages any project earning more than the cost of capital.
method: ROI = profit ÷ investment × 100 for each division.
Charge on capital = investment × cost of capital; RI = profit − charge.
Compare divisions on both measures and comment.
formula: ROI = Profit ÷ Investment × 100
Residual income = Profit − (Investment × Cost of capital)
topics.frame: Definition → types of centres (table) → importance → conclusion; for divisions, compute ROI and RI and rank them.
examples:
Example: ROI vs residual income
Division X: profit ₹3,00,000, investment ₹15,00,000 → ROI 20%. Division Y: profit ₹1,50,000, investment ₹5,00,000 → ROI 30%. Cost of capital 15%.
RI: X = 3,00,000 − 2,25,000 = ₹75,000; Y = 1,50,000 − 75,000 = ₹75,000.
Y is offered a project: investment ₹2,00,000, profit ₹50,000 (25%). It would cut Y's ROI to 2,00,000 ÷ 7,00,000 = 28.6%, so a manager judged on ROI may reject it. But it adds 50,000 − 30,000 = ₹20,000 to RI, and it is good for the company because 25% is above the 15% cost of capital.

topics.name: ABC, Target, Kaizen & Other Modern Costing
topics.summary: Activity-based costing, drawbacks of traditional costing, target costing, kaizen costing, throughput costing and value-chain analysis.
points: Activity-based costing (ABC): overheads are traced to activities and then to products using cost drivers. Steps: identify activities → build activity cost pools → choose cost drivers → compute driver rates → assign costs to products.
Advantages of ABC: more accurate product costs, better pricing and product-mix decisions, shows non-value-adding activities, suits many products and high overheads.
Drawbacks of traditional costing: one volume-based rate (labour or machine hours) distorts costs when products differ in complexity and batch size; ignores non-volume activities.
Target costing: target cost = target selling price − target profit. Steps: find market price → set required profit → compute target cost → design and value-engineer to reach it → keep costs there.
Kaizen costing: continuous small cost reductions during the production stage; features — employee involvement, small steps, all levels; approaches — asset-based and product-based.
Throughput costing: only direct materials treated as variable; throughput = sales − direct materials; focuses on bottlenecks.

Value-chain analysis (Porter): primary activities (inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, service) and support activities — used to find cost savings and competitive advantage.
Also in the book: life-cycle costing (all costs of a product from design to withdrawal), backflush costing (costs assigned only at the end of production, suited to JIT) and strategic cost management.
topics.frame: Definition → steps or features as headings → example → conclusion.
examples:
Example: ABC corrects a distorted cost
Set-up costs of ₹1,20,000 are shared by products A and B. A needs 10 set-ups and 8,000 labour hours; B needs 50 set-ups and 2,000 labour hours.
Traditional (labour hours): A ₹96,000, B ₹24,000.
ABC (driver = set-ups, ₹2,000 each): A ₹20,000, B ₹1,00,000.
B, made in many small batches, was being undercosted; ABC shows its true cost.

Example: target costing
Customers will pay ₹500 for a mixer-grinder; the company wants 20% profit on price (₹100), so the target cost is ₹400. The present design costs ₹450, so engineers must remove ₹50 — for example a simpler jar lid and a standard motor — before launch.

topics.name: Pricing Decisions
topics.summary: Internal and external factors influencing pricing decisions, methods of pricing, differentiated pricing and break-even pricing.
points: Internal factors: costs, company objectives, stage of product life cycle, marketing mix, product differentiation, organisation.
External factors: demand and elasticity, competition, customers and buyer behaviour, government regulation, economic conditions, suppliers, channel members.
Methods: cost-plus (full cost + markup), marginal-cost pricing, target-return pricing, going-rate pricing, penetration pricing, skimming, perceived-value pricing, sealed-bid pricing.
Differentiated pricing (price discrimination): different prices for customer groups, times, places or product forms.
Break-even pricing: setting the price at which revenue covers total cost at the expected volume.
topics.frame: Headed points with an Indian example each → conclusion.
examples:
Example: cost-plus vs marginal-cost pricing
Cost-plus: full cost of a table ₹800 + 25% markup → price ₹1,000.
Marginal-cost pricing: a hotel's variable cost per room-night is ₹1,200 and its normal rate ₹4,000. In the off-season it offers rooms to a tour group at ₹2,000. Each room still adds ₹800 of contribution towards fixed costs, which would otherwise earn nothing.

Example: differentiated pricing
A cinema charges less for weekday morning shows and gives student discounts; a railway charges different fares for sleeper and AC classes on the same train — different prices for times, groups and product forms.

topics.name: HRA, Social & Environmental Accounting
topics.summary: Human resource accounting, social accounting and social audit, environmental accounting and inflation accounting.
points: Human resource accounting (HRA): measuring and reporting the value of people in an organisation. Methods: historical cost, replacement cost, opportunity cost, present value of future earnings (Lev and Schwartz).
HRA suits people-intensive industries — IT, consulting, banking, education, healthcare. In India, companies such as BHEL and Infosys have reported it; it is relevant but voluntary.

Social accounting: measuring and reporting a firm's social costs and benefits. Social audit: steps — set objectives, identify stakeholders, collect data, assess performance, report, follow up; linked with CSR (Sec 135) and business responsibility reporting.
Environmental accounting: recording environmental costs, liabilities and benefits (pollution control, waste, resource use).
Inflation accounting: adjusting accounts for changing prices — current purchasing power (CPP) and current cost accounting (CCA) methods.
The book also covers international accounting and IT developments in accounting.
topics.frame: Meaning → methods or steps → relevance to India → conclusion.
examples:
Example: valuing an employee (Lev and Schwartz)
An employee will earn ₹6 lakh a year for the 3 years left before retirement; discount rate 10%.
Value = 6 × (1/1.1 + 1/1.1² + 1/1.1³) = 6 × 2.4869 = ₹14.92 lakh — the present value of future earnings used as the value of this human asset.

Example: inflation and environmental accounting
A machine bought for ₹10 lakh when the price index was 100 is shown at ₹10 lakh at cost; with the index now at 150, current purchasing power accounting restates it at ₹15 lakh, so depreciation and profit are not overstated in real terms.
A factory that spends on effluent treatment and pays a pollution fine records both separately as environmental costs, so management can see the cost of its environmental impact.
